SEC-HD-V8-01.note: Head is 'The shipment' (singular); 'blades'/'highlands' are proximity bait. 'since the war' forces present perfect. Only D is singular + perfect. The header states both halves, so the option set alone resolves it.

SEC-HD-V8-02.note: Supplement opened with a comma after 'The east range' must close with a comma, not a dash; head 'range' is singular. 2x2 grid, header names both axes.

SEC-HD-V8-03.note: 'who' is subject of 'had falsified'; 'the others believed' is parenthetical and does not make it an object. Four partners are named, so the clause identifies one and takes no commas. D is the trap that many editors would let pass, but it is non-restrictive; A doubles the error. Whom-after-a-parenthetical is common in speech but is not an edited-English convention, so I did not mark a second key.

SEC-HD-V8-04.note: 'Having lost the count' can only be predicated of a person, so the subject must be 'the observer'; the 1898 frame is closed, so simple past. Header gives both.

SEC-HD-V8-05.note: 'cut not only the number of stoppages' introduces a noun phrase, so 'but also' must be followed by a noun phrase. C and D re-supply a verb, breaking the parallel; B swaps the correlative. The header names the rule but you still have to look back at what 'not only' introduced.

SEC-HD-V8-06.note: 'more than one' takes a singular verb; the silting season is over, so simple past. C is defensible: 'more than one of' + plural noun with a plural verb is attested and accepted by some usage authorities on notional-agreement grounds, though the SAT convention is singular.

SEC-HD-V8-07.note: Two surveyors, so plural possessive 'surveyors''; restrictive 'that' takes no preceding comma. Header states both.

SEC-HD-V8-08.note: 'smell' as a linking verb takes the adjective 'sweet'; head is 'A cellar', singular, across the long relative clause. Both 'sweetly' options are eliminable on a general rule with no passage at all, which makes half the grid free.

SEC-HD-V8-09.note: 'each of' is singular and the resurveying precedes the 1861 request, so past perfect. D ('was already resurveyed') is genuinely defensible: simple past with 'already' is standard in edited American English when the sequence is clear from context, and D is also correct on number. This is the item where a strong student could reasonably split.

SEC-HD-V8-10.note: Gerund subject 'reconciling the entries...' is singular; 'In the years the wharf was in use' closes the frame, blocking the perfect.

SEC-HD-V8-11.note: 'as well as' does not compound the subject; head is 'The march', singular, and the retirement is a finished event, so simple past.

SEC-HD-V8-12.note: 'The tracings' is the head across 'along with'; the tracings are acted on, so passive. The two 'was/were losing' options are transitive-active with no object and read wrong without any passage.

SEC-HD-V8-13.note: Series is 'to sample... , to weight... , and ___', so the third member must be an infinitive. The header rules out the finite clause outright but you still have to read back to the earlier members to reject the two -ing forms.

SEC-HD-V8-14.note: Antecedent is 'The two presses', so 'their'; 'font' is the nearest-noun bait. The sale is a closed past event, so 'was'.

SEC-HD-V8-15.note: 'contains, in the same wallet as the awards themselves, a list of every hedge'. The interrupter must be closed after 'themselves'; nothing may separate 'a list' from 'of every hedge'. DEFECT: the word 'of' immediately after the blank kills C and D on its own, so the second half of the grid resolves from one word downstream.

SEC-HD-V8-16.note: The supplement 'a volume rebound so often...' must be closed with a comma, and 'records' cannot be separated from its object by a colon. DEFECT: 'three royal charters' right after the blank tells you a verb-plus-object is wanted, which by itself pushes off A and D.

SEC-HD-V8-17.note: Comma splice in A; the two clauses need a semicolon or a period. B (period + 'Consequently' with no comma) is defensible: a conjunctive adverb opening a sentence takes an optional comma in several major style guides, so B is not wrong under edited-English conventions. Only the header's explicit 'is followed by a comma' separates D from B, which makes this item depend on the header rather than on a convention the student could be expected to apply.

SEC-HD-V8-18.note: Proximity rule: the nearer subject is 'the village schoolmaster', singular; 'In the decade after' closes the frame, so simple past.

SEC-HD-V8-19.note: 'The remains' is plural-only; 'on about a dozen days a year' is a standing present fact. B/C/D each fail one axis.

SEC-HD-V8-20.note: Head is 'The clauses'; the relative clause ends on the singular 'width' as bait. 'for sixty years' from 1751 is a closed span, so simple past, not present perfect.

SEC-HD-V8-21.note: Counterfactual: 'If that manifest had reached... , the case would have collapsed'. The 'would have' belongs to the consequent only, so A double-marks it. The consequent is roughly ten words downstream, so this does not resolve inside four words, but a student scanning ahead gets it cheaply.

SEC-HD-V8-22.note: 'Because...' clause is closed with a comma; 'the lockers the yard had fitted' is a restrictive (reduced) relative and takes no commas. A omits the required intro comma; D over-punctuates.

SEC-HD-V8-23.note: 'reported in 1889 that...' backshifts 'will' to 'would'; the seam is the thing exhausted, so passive. 'would/will exhaust' misuse 'exhaust' intransitively and are eliminable with no passage.

SEC-HD-V8-24.note: 'one of the very few works of its kind that credit...' - the relative attaches to 'works', plural; restrictive, so no comma. B is defensible under the long-standing minority convention (and common editorial practice) of attaching the clause to 'one', giving 'that credits'. The header is what forces the plural, not anything in the sentence.

heuristics.name: present perfect is a distractor unless an explicit running-to-now span is printed
heuristics.rule: In every agreement item the grid crosses number against tense, and the perfect option is the key only when the passage prints 'since' or an equivalent open span. Every other passage opens with a closed frame ('In the season...', 'In the years...', 'In the decade after...', 'for sixty years', a dated event).
heuristics.hit_rate: 9/9 by my own reckoning - it is the key in 01 only, where 'since the war' appears, and a distractor in the other eight

heuristics.name: the head is the FIRST noun of the subject, never the nearest
heuristics.rule: Every agreement item interposes material of the opposite number between head and verb - a relative clause, 'along with', 'as well as', 'of the twelve tenants'. I never once had to think about which noun was the head; the construction announces it.

heuristics.name: in punctuation items the key has MATCHED marks or none
heuristics.rule: Reject any option that opens a supplement it does not close, closes one it did not open, or puts a mark between a noun and its own complement. This alone picked 02, 07, 15, 16, 22 and 24 without reading the sentence for sense.

heuristics.name: the 2x2 grid itself
heuristics.rule: 22 of 24 option sets are a clean 2x2 crossing exactly the two rules the header names. Once you know both rules, exactly one cell survives - there is never a third consideration. That regularity is itself a tell: a student who works out one axis has a 50 percent shot, and a student who reads the header has both axes handed over.

cross_item_heuristic.letter_distribution: My picks come out A:6 B:6 C:6 D:6, and no letter runs more than twice. Whatever else is wrong here, the key spread is clean and I found no positional tell.
cross_item_heuristic.verdict: The individual items are not guessable from each other's CONTENT, but the batch is highly guessable from its SHAPE. It was authored to one rigid brief - subject-verb distance bait crossed with a tense-frame cue, or a paired-mark boundary rule crossed with a second mark rule - and after four items I was solving by locating the two axes rather than by reading the passage. I read the full passage for real on 03, 05, 13, 15 and 16 only; on the other nineteen the stem fragment around the blank plus the option grid was enough.

header_summary.assessment: The headers did nearly all of the work, and I want to be blunt rather than modest about it. They do not merely name a skill - they state the rule AND its application, in the exact terms that discriminate the options. 'a singular head separated from its verb by a relative clause full of plurals, with the present perfect required by a span running to the present' is not a topic label; it is the answer, spelled out, before the passage is read. Cross it with a 2x2 option grid and exactly one cell survives. On 22 of 24 items I could have picked correctly from the header and the four options with the passage deleted entirely.
header_summary.worked_example: SEC-HD-V8-18. Header: verb agrees with the nearer subject, and a decade that is over will not take the present perfect. Options: have been / were / has been / was. Singular plus non-perfect is D, and no part of the passage is needed - not the topic, not the century, not which noun is nearer, because the header has already told me the nearer one governs.
header_summary.where_the_header_was_only_helpful: 05 and 13 are the two items where the header points at a rule but the passage still has to supply a fact: what kind of element 'not only' introduced (05) and what the earlier members of the series were (13). Those two are the shape the rest should have.
header_summary.load_bearing_cases: Two items depend on the header for something a strong student could legitimately dispute. On 17 only the header's 'an adverb opening the second clause is followed by a comma' separates D from B, since the comma after a sentence-initial conjunctive adverb is optional in several style guides. On 24 only the header's ruling that the clause agrees with the plural noun separates A from B, since attaching the clause to 'one' is a recognised minority convention. In both cases the header is not describing a rule the item independently enforces - it is legislating the disputed half.
header_summary.recommendation: If these headers ship attached to the items, the batch measures reading comprehension of the header. Strip them to a bare domain tag ('Standard English Conventions'), or at most name one axis, never both. If they are internal authoring metadata only, the finding instead is that the brief behind them is rigid enough to make the grid predictable on its own - see the cross-item heuristic.
